newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel and France bicker before Chirac's arrival.
newsitem.headline: Israel and France bicker before Chirac's arrival.

text.p: Israel and France bickered over one issue after another surrounding the visit by President Jacques Chirac even before he was due to set foot in the Jewish state on Monday.

Chirac, given a hero's welcome in Syria, declared Middle East peace in danger on Saturday and said Europe must join Washington in sponsoring Arab-Israeli negotiations, contributing proposals and not just money.

"A mediator entering into the conflict -- or into the negotiations -- is inconceivable," countered Foreign Minister David Levy on Sunday. "Every (outside) force that will enter into the negotiations puts obstacles into the negotiations."

Two other disputes, defused at the last minute, erupted over Chirac's plans to speak to Palestinian legislators while shunning Israel's parliament and to send his foreign minister to the disputed PLO headquarters in Arab East Jerusalem.

Arab leaders have welcomed European involvement in the U.S.-mediated peace talks but Israel has been reluctant to give Europeans an official role. Chirac's tour also takes him to Palestinian-ruled areas, Jordan, Lebanon and Egypt.
Israeli Ambassador to France Avi Pazner told Israel Radio that French relations had deepened with Israel in recent years but that Paris was traditionally close to the Arab world.

"I would be very careful before I would add more cooks to the broth," said right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, locked in U.S.-brokered talks with Palestinians on Israel's long-delayed pullback from the West Bank town of Hebron.

"The United States is playing a very important role as facilitator...and I don't think at this time in such sensitive negotiations it would be wise to introduce another interlocutor," Netanyahu said on a visit to an army base.

U.S. Middle East enjoy Dennis Ross spoke by phone with Israeli and Palestinian leaders throughout the weekend in mediation efforts to lock up a deal on a long overdue withdrawal from Hebron in the West Bank.
"There were intensive and serious talks until dawn but there are still no results," said PLO negotiator Hassan Asfour.

Syrian President Hafez al-Assad supported Chirac in Damascus, accusing Netanyahu's government of undermining peace moves since taking power four months ago on a platform opposed to swapping occupied Arab land for peace.

Knesset Speaker Dan Tichon, a member of the parliament from Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party, had said he would boycott Chirac's trip to Israel over the French president's failure to include the Knesset on his itinerary.
But Tichon said Chirac had changed his mind and would meet faction heads and sit in parliament during a visit on Tuesday.
"In the end they understood in France that they made a mistake and they're right to fix this mistake," Tichon said.
The French leader sparked the first diplomatic row with Israel even before setting off from Paris.
After the Israelis objected to his intention to send Foreign Minister Herve de Charette to PLO headquarters at Orient House, Chirac decided not to take de Charette to Israel at all.
Instead French junior health minister Herve Gaymard will visit in a move the Israelis grudgingly accepted behind the diplomatic fiction he will discuss health matters, not politics.
"At least the discomfort that would have been possible if the French foreign minister would visit Orient House was prevented," Netanyahu said.

Yet while Netanyahu swallowed that compromise, he may find Chirac's main message harder to digest -- that Israel can only hope for lasting security if it exchanges land for peace and allows a Palestinian state.
